plan.interpretation: The learner can explain core ML and backpropagation intuition, then write and run a PyTorch training loop for a small CNN image classifier and evaluate it for overfitting and accuracy.
assumptions: The 1200 minutes is pure viewing time, so it covers about 20 hours of videos with no time reserved for practice.
Because the learner likes code-along videos, the plan favors tutorials where the presenter writes code live.
'Small image classifier' means a CNN trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST or CIFAR-10, not a large pretrained model pipeline.
Each video or course part should fit within a 90-minute sitting, so long courses are picked in chunks of 90 minutes or less.
Calculus and linear algebra are already known, so math-focused videos should build intuition for ML and not reteach prerequisites.

sub_topics.title: Machine learning fundamentals: models, loss, features, train/test split
sub_topics.why: The learner has no ML background, so they need the vocabulary and framing (supervised learning, loss functions, generalization) before touching neural networks.

sub_topics.title: Gradient descent and backpropagation intuition and math
sub_topics.why: The learner knows calculus, so they can learn the chain rule applied to computation graphs and see how weights are updated, which gives the math intuition they want.

sub_topics.title: PyTorch tensors and autograd
sub_topics.why: The learner knows numpy, so tensors map to familiar ideas. They need to learn the PyTorch API, GPU/device handling, and how autograd computes gradients.

sub_topics.title: Building neural networks and training loops in PyTorch
sub_topics.why: They need to write nn.Module models, pick loss functions and optimizers, use DataLoaders and run the train/eval loop end to end.

sub_topics.title: Convolutional neural networks: convolutions, pooling, architectures
sub_topics.why: Image classification needs CNNs. A linear algebra background helps with understanding convolution as a sliding dot product and with feature maps and shapes.

sub_topics.title: Model evaluation, overfitting, and regularization
sub_topics.why: The learner must measure accuracy and tell whether the model generalizes, using validation splits, loss curves, confusion matrices, data augmentation, dropout and weight decay.

sub_topics.title: Build and train an image classifier end to end in PyTorch
sub_topics.why: A code-along project ties everything together: load an image dataset, build a CNN, train it, evaluate it, and iterate to improve results.

[00:00] Here we have some data points, and our goal is to train a curve that fits these points so we can predict outputs for new unseen data. Now, a single straight line can fit this data set, but it will be too simple to capture the pattern. This is called underfitting.
[00:20] On the other hand, if we try a very complex curve that fits the training data too well, the model ends up learning even the noise present in the data. As a result, it performs poorly on unseen data and does not generalize well. What we really want is a curve that's trained well, one that captures the true pattern in the data without learning the noise.
[00:45] Here is what typically happens during training. At first, both the training loss and the validation loss, that is, the loss on unseen data, starts decreasing. But after a certain point, while the training loss keeps going down, the validation loss starts increasing.
[01:43] That's the moment when the model begins to overfit. This is what we call overfitting. If you are not familiar with terms like training error, validation error, or overfitting, I've already made a detailed video on that topic. You can find the link in the description box below. Now, when a model is overfitting, we say it has high variance.
[02:07] So, our goal is to find a way to reduce that variance. In other words, to fix the problem of overfitting. And this is where regularization comes into the picture. Regularization is anything we do to prevent overfitting and help the model generalize better. Now, when we train a model for too long or make it too complex, it often ends up with large weight values.
[02:33] That's because the model is trying too hard to fit every single data point, even the noisy ones. So it adjusts its parameters drastically to minimize the training loss.
[03:24] In contrast, simpler models usually have smaller weights since they focus only on the main trends in the data, rather than the tiny fluctuations. So our goal is to train a model in such a way that the weights don't grow too large. Keeping the weights small helps prevent the model from reacting too strongly to the noise, and that's exactly what regularization helps us achieve.
[03:49] Now, let's take mean squared error as the base cost function. To control the size of our weights, we will modify this loss function slightly. We create a new loss function by adding an extra term called the penalty term. This penalty term is controlled by a hyperparameter called lambda, also known as the regularization hyperparameter.
[04:11] When lambda is bigger, the penalty is bigger; when lambda is smaller, the penalty is smaller. It's a fixed value that decides how strongly we want to penalize large weights.
[05:02] The penalty itself is the sum of squares of all the weights, which is known in mathematics as the L2 norm. So, when we add this L2 penalty term to our loss, this is called L2 regularization. During training, the optimizer tries to minimize the total loss, which now includes both the original loss and the penalty.
[05:25] Since large weights increase the penalty, the optimizer naturally prefers smaller weights. They help reduce the total loss without hurting the fit too much. This will be clear in a moment using geometry. But before that, let's see another type of regularization, called the L1 regularization. Here we use the L1 norm, where we only take the norm of weights without squaring it.
[05:50] Now, when we optimize the new loss function, we take derivatives with respect to the weights. In the L1 case, the derivative of the penalty term depends on the sign of the weights, meaning it contributes a constant factor to the gradient, regardless of the weight's magnitude.
[06:47] In contrast, in the L2 case, the derivative is proportional to the weight itself. So, larger weights produce larger gradients, and smaller weights produce smaller gradients. This term is then used during weight updates in gradient descent. It's this contribution that effectively shrinks the weights while training, helping the model avoid overfitting.
[07:10] Now, do not get confused by all the math and derivatives. Let's look at this geometrically, which could be easier to understand. Let's visualize this using just two weights W1 and W2 because it's easier to see in two dimensions. For these two weights, the norms looks like this. The original mean squared cost function, without any penalty, forms elliptical contours.
[07:35] The point at the center, let's call it W1 star and W2 star, is where the original loss is minimized.

Want to map your data analysis process clearly? Try Wondershare EdrawMax ：https://event.wondershare.com/api/s/3Mj

A very simple explanation of convolutional neural network or CNN or ConvNet such that even a high school student can understand it easily. This video involves very less math and is perfect for total beginner who doesn't have any idea on what CNN is and how it works. We will cover different topics such as,

1. Why traditionally humans are better at image recognition than computers?
2. Disadvantages of using traditional artificial neural network (ANN) for image classification.
3. How human brain recognizes images?
4. How computers can use filters for feature detection
5. What is convolution operation and how it works
6. Importance of ReLU activation in CNN
7. Importance of pooling operation in CNN
8. How to handle rotation and scale in CNN

pool.description:
# Curing Overfitting with Regularization | Season 1 | Part 29

🚀 Welcome to **Curing Overfitting with Regularization | Season 1 | Part 29**!

In this episode, you'll learn how to recognize and fix one of the most common problems in Machine Learning and Deep Learning: **overfitting**.

A Neural Network can perform extremely well on its training data while struggling with images or examples it has never seen before. Regularization helps solve this problem by encouraging the model to learn meaningful patterns instead of simply memorizing the training dataset.

Using PyTorch, you'll explore the most important regularization techniques and understand how they improve a model's ability to generalize to unseen data.

📚 In this video you'll learn:
• What is overfitting?
• Training performance vs validation performance
• How to recognize an overfitted Neural Network
• Why complex Deep Learning models overfit
• Understanding regularization
• L1 and L2 regularization
• Weight decay in PyTorch
• How Dropout prevents overfitting
• Choosing an appropriate Dropout probability
• Data augmentation for Computer Vision
• Early stopping during model training
• Reducing unnecessary model complexity
• Combining multiple regularization techniques
• Measuring improvements on validation data
• Building models that generalize to unseen data

You'll also understand an important Deep Learning principle: **the best model isn't necessarily the one with the lowest training loss. It's the model that performs reliably on new, unseen data.**

💡 **Acknowledgement:**
Some of the concepts and learning approaches discussed in this series are inspired by the educational work of **@AndrejKarpathy**. If you want to deepen your understanding of Neural Networks, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning, check out the **@AndrejKarpathy** YouTube channel for excellent educational content.

This is **Season 1, Part 29** of the **Deep Learning Foundations** series, where you'll continue building the practical knowled

[00:00] You build a neural network, you start training, and your accuracy climbs perfectly toward 99%. But when you test it on new data, the performance flatlines entirely. Your network hasn't learned the task, it has just memorized the answers to the test. We are going to fix that. We'll take a PyTorch model that fails under its own weight and systematically repair it using batch normalization, spatial dropout, and data augmentation.
[00:27] To follow along with this interactive experiment, you will need a basic understanding of PyTorch syntax and an active Google Colab environment. An unregularized network will use its processing power to memorize the exact pixel values of your training data. True generalization, the ability to perform accurately on data the model has never seen before, is the only metric that matters when you move a project out of the lab and into production.
[00:51] This grid displays our target, the Fashion M nest data set. It consists of thousands of 28x28 pixel grayscale images sorted into 10 distinct clothing classes.
[01:43] This chart plots our learning rate strategy. We are using a lambda LR scheduler, mathematically decaying the rate from 0.001 steadily toward zero over 60 epochs to stabilize the training process. Before trying to fix a complex network, we need to prove our setup works. This code block shows our sanity check, a lightweight sequential architecture.
[02:07] We pass a single isolated batch of data through this small model to test its raw capacity. This graph maps the results of that single batch test. The blue loss curve drops perfectly to zero, and the orange training accuracy hits 1.0. The model successfully memorizes the batch. If a network fails this specific test, it lacks the raw mathematical capacity to learn the target rules, a condition known as high bias.
[02:30] If a model is underfitting this severely, advanced regularization techniques will not save it. Because our model passed, we can confidently scale up.
[03:19] We now switch to a deeper medium architecture to increase our processing power. Look at the parameter documentation here. For our first run on the full data set, we leave use batch norm, use spatial dropout, and use combined set to false. We are running raw and unprotected. These plots show the immediate failure of that approach.
[03:39] The blue training loss drops predictably, but the orange validation loss climbs aggressively. This diverging space is the overfitting gap, confirming the network stops learning universal properties and starts memorizing specific training noise. Scaling up a model's parameter count without imposing internal boundaries guarantees high variance.
[04:00] The network becomes highly confident on familiar data, but dangerously brittle on everything else. To fight that variance, we apply spatial dropout. Instead of turning off individual neurons, this technique randomly drops entire two-dimensional feature maps from the convolutional layers during training. It forces the network to find alternate redundant patterns instead of relying on a single visual crutch.
[05:03] But even when we combine dropout with batch normalization to stabilize the internal math, the results are incomplete. The validation loss improves slightly, but the overfitting gap remains clearly visible. We need to look outside the architecture itself. This is data augmentation. By applying random horizontal flips, rotations, and zooms on the fly, we transform a single training sample into infinite unique variations.
[05:31] This chart captures the results of using data augmentation alone. Notice how the orange validation loss flattens out significantly, tracking much closer to the training line. By artificially expanding the structural variety of the training data, we provide the network with a much wider empirical foundation. For image classification, this external variance is often the most powerful stand-alone tool you have.
[05:56] Now we activate all three protocols simultaneously, data augmentation, batch normalization, and dropout.
[06:43] Look at the loss plot for Experiment 7. The overfitting gap is practically eliminated. The validation loss drops smoothly and remains stable directly alongside the training loss. Individual techniques offer incremental gains, but moving a system from simple memorization to reliable production-grade generalization requires this kind of synergistic stack.
[07:06] This chart plots validation loss across eight permutations. The top two lines are unregularized models, visualize the severe penalty of scaling without controlling variance. The lowest pink line, Experiment 7, proves the cumulative power of layering data augmentation with architectural constraints. With a verified stable framework, the next step is yours.
[07:28] Apply these exact same techniques to the larger, more complex architectures in Experiment 8, and test how far you can push generalization on your own data sets.

The inability for a machine learning method (like linear regression) to capture the true relationship is called Bias.
[03:44] Because the Straight Line can't be curved like the “true” relationship, it has a relatively large amount of bias. Another machine learning method might fit a Squiggly Line to the training set… The Squiggly Line is super flexible and hugs the training set along the arc of the true relationship.
[04:05] Because the Squiggly Line can handle the arc in the true relationship between weight and height, it has very little bias. We can compare how well the Straight Line and the Squiggly Line fit the training set by calculating their sums of squares.

For such a model, we say that is overfitted and it is unable to generalize well to the new data. Yes, it has learned the features of the training set extremely well, but if we give the model any data that slightly deviates from the exact data used during training, it is unable to generalize and accurately predict the accurately predict the output.

[03:27] The logical response to prevent overfitting can either be to stop the training process earlier or to reduce complexity of the network. However, in both of these cases, the opposite problem called underfitting can occur. It happens when the model has not trained for enough time, so it is unable to determine a meaningful relationship between the input and output variables.

pool.title: [ML1] Machine Learning Fundamentals: Supervised Learning & Linear Regression
pool.description:
In this video, we break down what machine learning actually is from the ground up, moving from intuitive concepts to mathematical foundations.   

Whether you're starting your ML journey or building a solid conceptual core, this video covers the fundamental triad of supervised learning: model representation, loss functions and optimization.
   
TIMESTAMPS:
0:00 - Introduction to Machine Learning & Real-World Prediction   
1:30 - Supervised Learning & The Prediction Equation
4:04 - Linear Regression & Parameter Notation (Weights & Biases)   
6:07 - Feature Vectors & Design Matrices   
7:36 - Loss Functions & Mean Squared Error (MSE)   
9:04 - Optimization via Gradient Descent & Learning Rates   
10:06 - Generalization, Validation, and Overfitting

[00:00] Hi Sen here. Today we'll be learning about what machine learning actually is, how we represent it mathematically and what it means for a model to learn from data. Let's start with a simple example. Suppose we're trying to predict the price of a house. We have information about 1,000 houses that were sold previously. We know their area, the number of bedrooms, how old they are and their actual selling prices.
[00:23] Now, suppose someone gives us information about a new house and asks us to predict its price. How would we approach this? One way would be to examine the historical data and try to identify relationships between the characteristics of a house and its price. For example, we might notice that larger houses generally sell for higher prices.
[00:43] But knowing that relationship exists isn't enough. We also need to understand how strongly the size of a house affects its price and how that relationship changes when other features are involved. Rather than manually defining all these relationships, we want to learn them from the available data. That's the fundamental idea behind supervised machine learning.
[01:41] We have examples of inputs and their corresponding outputs, and we're trying to learn a mathematical function that makes useful predictions on new inputs. Now, notice something important here. We're trying to learn a function. In mathematics, a function takes an input and produces an output. We generally represent that as y equals f of x.
[02:04] But in machine learning, we don't necessarily know what the correct function looks like. So we introduce a more useful representation. Y hat equals f theta of x. This is one of the most fundamental equations in machine learning. Let's understand what each symbol means. First, X represents our input features. In our example, these could be the characteristics of a house.
[02:28] Next, F represents our model, which is the mathematical function we're using to make predictions. Then we have theta, which represents the parameters that control how the function behaves.
[03:19] And finally, y hat represents the prediction produced by our model. We distinguish y hat from y because y is the actual value, while y hat is what the model predicts. Now, let's understand what parameters actually represent. You probably remember the equation of a straight line from school, y equals mx plus c.
[03:40] Here M represents the slope and C represents the intercept. If we change m, we change the slope of the line. If we change C, we shift the line up or down. But regardless of what values we choose, we are still working with a straight line. That's an important idea.
[04:01] We have a family of mathematical functions and the parameters determine which particular function we are using. Machine learning works similarly. We choose a family functions, often called a model class, and use data to learn suitable parameters. For example, let's assume that house prices are approximately linearly related to house size. We can represent our model as y hat equals wx plus b.
[05:05] Here, W represents the weight and B represents the bias. These are the parameters that our model needs to learn. If W is positive, increasing the size of the house increases its predicted price. If W is negative, increasing the size decreases its predicted price. And B controls where our prediction line intersects the vertical axis.
[05:27] This model is called linear regression. Now something worth understanding is that the model isn't learning what a straight line is. We've already chosen that representation. The model is learning which straight line best fits the relationship in our data. And by choosing a linear model, we've also made an assumption that a straight line is a reasonable approximation of the relationship we're trying to predict.
[05:50] We'll come back to why this assumption matters. So far, we've used only one input feature, house size. But what if we want to consider the number of bedrooms, the age of the house and its location?

pool.title: PyTorch a framework for research of dynamic deep learning models - Adam Paszke
pool.description:
PyTorch: a framework for research of dynamic deep learning models. How, why, and what's next?
Adam Paszke

Description
PyTorch is one of deep learning frameworks that can natively support models without a predefined structure, and is now widely used at companies and universities all around the world. The talk aims to introduce its basic tensor library, automatic differentiation package, a set of helpers for constructing novel machine learning models, and discuss the future of the library.

Abstract
So, why do we need dynamical computational graphs again?
Recently, there's been a rising interest in frameworks that can support dynamical computational graphs natively and there's a reason for that. This section will introduce the concept and discuss pros and cons compared to static graph frameworks.

Ok, show me the code
This is meant to showcase the different levels of abstraction at which PyTorch can be used. Here I'll start with the lowest one, which is a NumPy-like tensor library. No fancy features; Just a good old imperative paradigm sprinkled with some linear algebra (on GPUs too!).

Automatic differentiation to the rescue!
While having a NumPy alternative with a fast GPU backend is great, it still doesn't allow you to easily experiment with machine learning models. This section introduces torch.autograd - a package allowing to wrap tensors and automatically track their usage so as to compute derivatives of expressions automatically.

High-level helpers
Automatic differentiation is a huge leap forward, but writing out more complicated models can get pretty verbose. torch.nn has been created just for this purpose. It features over a hundred commonly used building blocks (not only for neural networks), just so that you can compose your model in a handful of lines.

Extending the library
So far so good, but we're talking about a research library. It's not always sufficient to rely on what has been provided for you. Also, there's no point in having the whole Python pa

pool.title: Underfitting & Overfitting - Explained
pool.description:
Underfitting and overfitting are some of the most common problems you encounter while constructing a statistical/machine learning model. It is therefore important to be able to recognize when either is occurring and what can be done to fix it. This is an extremely brief overview covering those topics, and, as always in machine learning, there is more to learn.

Resources for Further Study:

More in-depth look at fixing underfitting and overfitting 
- https://towardsdatascience.com/overfitting-and-underfitting-principles-ea8964d9c45c#:~:text=Underfitting%20means%20that%20your%20model,val%2Ftest%20error%20is%20large.
(Note: this author states that more data will not help with underfitting, however this is mainly true when you already have a bad model. If you are working with significantly less data (100s or 1000s of data points) then getting more data will make a bigger impact on underfitting.)

A full example of underfitting and overfitting
-https://towardsdatascience.com/overfitting-vs-underfitting-a-complete-example-d05dd7e19765

[00:00] Let's get right into it. In machine learning, the basic premise is that you provide a model with training data to predict a target variable, and then, with a little algorithmic magic, your model spits out its predictions. What you want is for your model to be able to then take in new data and make new predictions.
[00:20] However, you can and will run into many issues on your way. Two of the most common problems are underfitting and overfitting. Underfitting usually occurs when your model hasn't had enough time or data to train with, and, as a result, it cannot pick up on the general patterns needed to make accurate predictions.
[00:44] It can also be the result of a mismatch model, say, trying to fit a line to data that is in reality distributed along a quadratic. You can generally resolve this problem by picking a different model, increasing the amount of time or iterations the model trains for, or using more training data.
[01:43] While underfitting is quite straightforward, overfitting tends to be less intuitive. Overfitting essentially occurs when your model is too accurate. What this means in practice is that the model has learned patterns that are only in the training data. Effectively, using the random noise that arises in real-world samples to make predictions.
[02:07] This is obviously a problem because our new data will almost certainly not feature the patterns and noise our model uses, and, as a result, new predictions will be markedly less accurate. You can look for overfitting quite easily by comparing the error amounts between training data and validation data, validation data being data you haven't used to train the model already.
[02:31] Here, you can see an example of the accuracy, mean absolute error, and mean squared error that might occur for an overfitting model.
[03:22] If you see that your results look highly accurate for your training data, but terrible for your validation data, then you are looking at overfitting. To resolve overfitting, you will often need to graph out the accuracy of your model with different hyperparameters and see which ones produce the highest validation accuracy.
[03:43] Although, be forewarned that this can drastically increase the time it takes to train your model. Given that this is a very brief overview of these problems, I would encourage you to research the methods used to deal with underfitting and especially overfitting further. And better yet, put them into practice with an actual data set.
[04:04] Well, that looks like all the time I have. Thanks for watching, and I wish you luck in your future data endeavors.

When implementing adversarial attacks like PGD (Projected Gradient Descent) on face detection models such as S3FD using PyTorch, you might encounter this common error during backpropagation:

[00:00] Fixing loss.backward() Gradient Issues in PyTorch S3FD PGD Attack Understanding Gradient Errors in PyTorch PGD Attacks with S3FD When implementing adversarial attacks like PGD (Projected Gradient Descent) on face detection models such as S3FD using PyTorch, you might encounter this common error during backpropagation:
[00:27] RuntimeError: element 0 of tensors does not require grad and does not have a grad_fn This means the loss tensor you are calling loss.backward() on does not track gradients, breaking the gradient flow. Root Cause: Breaking the Computational Graph Your implementation uses a face detector that:
[00:47] Runs detection and outputs predictions as NumPy arrays. Performs operations involving NumPy and Python loops. This conversion from PyTorch tensors to NumPy arrays detaches the result from PyTorch's autograd system. Consequently, tensors derived from these NumPy arrays do not require gradients.
[01:49] For example, in your batch_detect function (from detect.py): olist = [oelem.data.cpu().numpy() for oelem in olist] Here, .data and .numpy() forcefully detach tensors from the graph. Later, you build loss using elements like pred_conf which are created from these NumPy arrays (converted back to tensors), so they have requires_grad=False.
[02:15] Why Does This Matter? Only tensors with: requires_grad=True Connected upstream to the model parameters through differentiable ops. Will allow backpropagation via loss.backward(). If intermediate tensors are detached or NumPy arrays, gradients will not flow backward.
[02:38] How to Fix the Issue 1. Preserve Tensors without NumPy Conversion
[03:26] Avoid converting your model outputs to NumPy when you want to compute losses and gradients. Work within PyTorch tensors all along. Update batch_detect Remove .data and .numpy() calls. Return raw PyTorch Tensors. 2. Rewrite Loss Computation in PyTorch
[03:47] Instead of building pred_conf from NumPy arrays, maintain them as tensors. Ensure pred_conf has requires_grad=True if derived from model outputs. Use PyTorch tensor operations inside your loss function. 3. Check Inputs to Loss and Whether They Require Grad
[04:08] Add debug prints before backward pass. print('Loss requires grad:', loss.requires_grad) for i in potential_true_index: print(f'pred_conf[{i}].requires_grad:', pred_conf[i].requires_grad)
[04:59] If any is False, investigate earlier steps. 4. Avoid Detached Copies Your code creates new tensors from NumPy arrays (e.g., pred_conf = torch.tensor(pred_conf, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)), which defaults to requires_grad=False. Instead, keep all computation in tensors deriving directly from the model's outputs.
[05:29] Summary Checklist [x] Do not convert intermediate model outputs to NumPy for loss computation [x] Rewrite detection post-processing to maintain tensors on PyTorch graph [x] Ensure variables participating in loss have requires_grad=True
[05:49] [x] Verify gradients flow by checking .requires_grad flag before .backward() By following these steps, your loss.backward() call will correctly accumulate gradients in perturbation_grad, enabling your PGD attack to function correctly.
[06:47] This is a common pitfall when mixing PyTorch and NumPy — always be mindful to preserve the computation graph when gradients are needed.

Users rapidly adopted PyTorch 1.0 for many reasons. PyTorch is intuitive to learn, and its modularity enhances debugging and visibility. We’ll also discuss pre-release serialization and performance issues, as well as the increased focus on optimization and performance in PyTorch 1.0.
